problem: The rule as written states the conclusion in its own premise and then contradicts itself. It says "if process j has to roll back to a checkpoint taken before it received a message m ... then j's checkpoint holds an orphan and is invalid. Process j rolls back further." If j has already rolled back to a checkpoint before the receive, no receive of m is in that checkpoint, so it cannot be an orphan; and "rolls back further" then makes no sense. The cause (j's current checkpoint contains the receive, the sender's chosen checkpoint misses the send) and the effect (j must discard that checkpoint and go back to one before the receive) are swapped. A student cannot follow the domino chain from this sentence.
fix: The rollback rule: if process j's checkpoint contains the receive of a message m, and m was sent by process i after the checkpoint i has chosen, then the recovered run has the receive but not the send. j's checkpoint holds an orphan and is invalid, so j rolls back to a checkpoint taken before it received m. That rollback can itself invalidate a checkpoint of a third process, and the chain continues.

problem: The C3,1 bar runs from t = 11 to t = 12.5, so the write is still in progress when P1 crashes at t = 12. The worked example treats C3,1 as a completed checkpoint taken at t = 11 that P3 rolls back from, and never mentions an interrupted write. Figure and text disagree.
fix: End the C3,1 bar at t = 11 (or move the crash time to t = 13) so the figure shows a completed checkpoint, matching the example.

problem: "Piecewise deterministic, meaning its state changes only when a message arrives" is not the standard definition. A process also changes state during local computation; what makes it piecewise deterministic is that every nondeterministic event is a message reception and the execution between such events is deterministic. As written, a student could think a process doing long local computation does not fit the model.
fix: Each process is piecewise deterministic: every nondeterministic event it meets is the reception of a message, and between two such events its execution is deterministic. A saved state plus the received messages in their logged order therefore rebuilds the state exactly.

problem: "Communication-induced, or quasi-synchronous, checkpointing" treats two terms as exact synonyms. Quasi-synchronous checkpointing is a family inside communication-induced checkpointing (checkpoints grouped into quasi-synchronous intervals); equating them will confuse a student who meets both names in an exam question.
fix: Communication-induced checkpointing sends no extra control messages: each application message carries a few piggybacked numbers about its sender's checkpoints, and the receiver takes a forced checkpoint when delivery would otherwise make its latest checkpoint inconsistent. Quasi-synchronous protocols are one family within this class.

problem: "Databases use logging rather than rollback, in the redo and undo style of ARIES" is misleading: ARIES does roll back (undo) uncommitted transactions; what it avoids is rolling back to an old checkpoint of the whole database. The phrase as written suggests databases never undo work.
fix: Databases use logging with undo and redo, in the style of ARIES: committed work is redone from the log and uncommitted work is undone, instead of restoring a whole-database checkpoint.
